criterion_notes.c1: Chapter 1 explicitly frames the book around urban residents' access to piped drinking water supply in China and India (including coverage of connections, hours per day of supply, and per capita water supply).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study clearly qualifies (yes) because it examines informal and formal governance, institutional autonomy and capacity, decentralization, state ownership vs. PPPs, and urban water laws and regulations. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is unclear from the retrieved text alone: the overarching independent variable presented in Chapter 1 ('types of social contracts': performance/mandate of heaven vs. socialism and populism) is an informal macro-governance/political-economy factor that fails the narrow rule-type scope on its own, whereas the missing Chapters 5–7 (DOI 10.1017/9781108580373, of which only Chapter 1 DOI 10.1017/9781108580373.001 was retrieved) examine urban water laws and regulations, utility ownership/PPPs vs. state ownership, municipal regulatory restructuring, cost recovery, and populist promises of free water—mechanisms that could fall within the rule-type scope if empirically linked to service access in Part II.
criterion_notes.c3: Only Chapter 1 (pp. 1–27, DOI 10.1017/9781108580373.001) of the book (DOI 10.1017/9781108580373) is present in the retrieved PDF. Chapter 1 cites secondary national/benchmark summary statistics (Tables 1.1 and 1.2) to pose the puzzle, while explicitly stating that Chapter 2 explains case selection and methodology and Part II (Chapters 5–7) provides the empirical evidence. Without Chapters 2 and 5–7, empirical methods and primary/case-study evidence cannot be verified.
criterion_notes.c4: Chapter 1 reports national/multi-city benchmark urban water access outcomes (piped water coverage, continuity in hours per day, per capita supply in liters/capita-day, metering, and cost recovery in Tables 1.1 and 1.2), although the city-level empirical outcomes for Beijing, Shenzhen, New Delhi, and Hyderabad in Chapters 6–7 are missing from the PDF.
criterion_notes.c5: Because only Chapter 1 of the book was retrieved and Chapter 2 ('case selection and methodology for testing my theory') and Part II (Chapters 5–7) are missing, the study design, data collection methods, and empirical operationalization of city-level exposures and outcomes cannot be determined from the provided text (failing Criterion 8 accessibility for methodological assessment).
criterion_notes.c6: The text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study examines one aspect of public goods provision – the supply of drinking water to urban residents. Why do most Chinese urban residents have uninterrupted access to drinking water while only a little more than half of Indian urban residents have access to two to three hours of piped water supply per day?
India’s urban population does not have continuous access to piped water (Table 1.1). In 2011, urban residents in India had access to piped water for only two hours per day.

A social contract encapsulates a certain set of ideas, principles, and precepts that guide and inform the actions of state actors and ordinary citizens of a country, helping to explain the different outcomes in public goods provision.

It then examines the impact of social contracts on the design of formal institutions, which in turn affects the government’s ability to produce public goods. It also explains my case selection and methodology for testing my theory.
Part II provides the empirical evidence that supports my argument.
It compares and contrasts the water institutional frameworks in China and India in terms of bureaucratic structures, laws, policies, and regulations that govern the urban water sectors.

raw_response.exposure: Types of national social contracts (performance-based in China vs. socialist and populist in India) shaping formal urban water governance institutions, bureaucratic capacity/autonomy, state ownership vs. private sector participation (PPPs), and water sector laws, regulations, and tariff/free-water policies
raw_response.outcome: Urban drinking water access and service indicators: piped water connection coverage, continuity of supply (hours per day), per capita water supply (liters/capita-day), nonrevenue water/water loss, metering, and cost recovery
raw_response.population_and_sample: Urban residents and urban water sectors in China and India (case studies of Shenzhen, Beijing, New Delhi, and Hyderabad are previewed for Chapters 6–7, which are missing from the retrieved PDF)
